prompt: With spanning tree off, a broadcast went round the lab's triangle until the cable was pulled. Why did it not die out by itself?
hint: Compare an Ethernet frame with an IP packet.

choices.text: The switches lowered its TTL, but 255 laps take a while
choices.why: Switches do not touch a TTL. That field is in the IP header, and routers lower it.

choices.text: An Ethernet frame has no hop count to run out
choices.why: Right. A switch forwards the frame unchanged, so a copy that goes round is as fresh as when it started.

choices.text: Each PC kept sending the broadcast again because no reply came back
choices.why: Nobody typed anything during those three seconds. The copies came from the switches flooding.

choices.text: Each switch sent it back out of the port it arrived on
choices.why: Flooding leaves out the arrival port. The loop comes from the third switch, not from a frame bounced back.

prompt: Before the loop, sw1's p2 had received 21 packets. Three seconds of loop later the same counter read 201975. How many frames arrived on that port in between?
hint: Subtract the before from the after.

prompt: Two switches are joined by two cables and spanning tree is off. Which of these follow? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two cables between two switches are a loop of length two.

choices.text: Broadcasts circulate between the two switches and multiply
choices.why: Yes. Each switch floods what it receives on one cable out of the other.

choices.text: A PC's MAC address moves back and forth between ports in the MAC tables
choices.why: Yes. Copies of its frames arrive on both cables, so the table keeps changing its mind.

choices.text: The link between them doubles its capacity
choices.why: Doubling needs link aggregation, lesson 21. Without it, two cables are a loop.

choices.text: The second cable stays idle as a spare until the first one fails
choices.why: That is what spanning tree arranges. With it switched off, both cables forward.

prompt: During a broadcast storm, frames for pc2 sometimes leave sw1 by the wrong port. What causes that?
hint: Think about how a switch learns which port a MAC is behind.

choices.text: The storm corrupts the destination MAC in the frames
choices.why: The frames are copied intact. The destination is right; the table is what is wrong.

choices.text: sw1 runs out of space in its MAC table and forgets pc2
choices.why: A forgotten address would be flooded, not sent out of one wrong port.

choices.text: pc2 answers ARP from two different MAC addresses
choices.why: pc2 has one network card and one MAC. The duplication is in the switches.

choices.text: Copies of pc2's frames arrive on both p2 and p3, so sw1 keeps moving pc2's entry
choices.why: Right. That is MAC flapping: the entry points at whichever port the last copy came in on.

prompt: The three switches report these bridge IDs. Which one becomes the root?
hint: Lowest wins, priority first.

choices.why: That is the highest of the three MACs, and the priorities tie.
Lower than sw2's, but 02:6a comes before 02:a5.
Right. Equal priorities, so the lowest MAC, sw1's, wins.

choices.text: Neither yet: three equal priorities wait for an administrator to pick one
choices.why: A tie on priority is broken by the MAC address, with no human involved.

prompt: A bridge ID starts with 8000, the default priority written in hexadecimal. What is it in decimal?
Switches running STP exchange small frames called ___, by default one every 2 seconds.
hint: Bridge protocol data units.

prompt: sw2 reports root_port:1 and root_path_cost:2. Every port in the lab costs 2. What does the 2 tell you?
hint: Cost is added per port along the path.

choices.text: sw2 is two cables away from the root
choices.why: Two cables would add two port costs, which is 4 here.

choices.text: sw2 is one cable away from the root
choices.why: Right. One port at cost 2 lies between sw2 and the root.

choices.text: sw2 has two ports in forwarding state
choices.why: Path cost measures distance to the root, not how many ports forward.

choices.text: sw2 was the second switch to be elected
choices.why: There is one election, for the root. The others are not ranked.

prompt: Put the 802.1D states in the order a port passes through them on its way into use.
hint: Two waits of 15 seconds sit in the middle.
trap: Learning before listening is the usual slip: the port first waits for the election to settle, and fills its MAC table after that.

prompt: Match each port role to what it does.
hint: Think of the triangle after the election.

pairs.right: A non-root switch's cheapest way to the root
The end of a cable that forwards onto it
Listens to BPDUs and forwards no data

right_distractors: Carries the root's MAC address in its bridge ID

prompt: On the sw2–sw3 cable both ends are one cable from the root sw1, at cost 2. Why does sw2's end block rather than sw3's?
hint: When costs tie, something else is compared.

choices.text: sw3's bridge ID is lower, so sw3's end is designated
choices.why: Right. 02a59d312a8c is lower than 02e0779de790, and the tie goes to the lower ID.

choices.text: sw3 has a PC on p10 and sw2 does not
choices.why: Both have a PC on p10, and PCs play no part in the election.

choices.text: sw2's p3 was plugged in last, so it waits
choices.why: The cable plugged in last was sw3 to sw1, and order of plugging does not decide roles.

choices.text: Port 3 loses to port 2 because the lower port number is preferred
choices.why: Port numbers break ties between ports of one switch, not between two switches.

prompt: A port has just moved from listening to learning. What is it doing for the next 15 seconds?
hint: The name says what it does; the table says what it does not.

choices.text: Forwarding data while it checks for loops
choices.why: Forwarding comes after learning. Checking for loops while forwarding is what classic STP avoids.

choices.text: Filling its MAC table from arriving frames, forwarding no data
choices.why: Right. When it starts forwarding it already knows where addresses are.

choices.text: Waiting in silence, sending no BPDUs
choices.why: A learning port does send and receive BPDUs.

choices.text: Re-running the root election
choices.why: The election goes on in BPDUs whatever the state; learning is about MAC addresses.

prompt: On sw3, ip -d link show p1 prints designated_bridge 8000.2:6a:dc:93:3b:8a. What does that make p1?
hint: Whose bridge ID is that, with the zeros put back?

choices.text: sw3's root port: the designated end is the root, sw1
choices.why: Right. 8000.026adc933b8a is sw1, so p1 is the way to the root.

choices.text: A designated port, because the field names it
choices.why: The field names the designated end of the cable, which is on another switch.

choices.text: A blocked port, since another bridge is designated on its cable
choices.why: The other end being designated does not make this end blocked: here this end leads to the root.

choices.text: A disabled port, because the MAC is printed without zeros
choices.why: Dropping leading zeros is just how ip prints it. The port's state was forwarding.

prompt: Under classic STP, how many seconds does a blocked port spend in listening and learning together before it forwards, with default timers?
hint: Two forward delays.

prompt: pc2 pinged pc1 once a second for 60 seconds while the sw1–sw2 cable was pulled. The summary said 60 transmitted, 30 received. How many echo requests went unanswered?
hint: Transmitted minus received.

prompt: sw3's priority is set to 4096, so sw3 becomes the root. Which port in the triangle blocks now?
hint: Find the cable furthest from the new root, then break the tie.

choices.text: sw2's p3, as before
choices.why: That cable now touches the root, so sw3's end of it is designated and sw2's p3 is sw2's root port.

choices.text: sw2's p1
choices.why: Right. On the sw1–sw2 cable the costs tie, sw1's lower ID makes its end designated, and sw2's end blocks.

choices.text: sw1's p2, because sw1 lost the election
choices.why: Losing the root election does not block a port by itself. sw1 still has the lower ID of the two on that cable.

choices.text: sw3's p1, the cable to the old root
choices.why: Ports on the root are designated, so sw3 has no port to block.

prompt: Match each 802.1D timer to its default.
A cable fails two switches away, so a switch notices only because BPDUs stop arriving. With default timers, about how many seconds pass before its blocked port forwards?
hint: Max age first, then the two forward delays.

prompt: Which IEEE standard introduced Rapid Spanning Tree?
hint: A letter after 802.1, published in 2001.

choices.why: That is VLAN tagging, lesson 19, and today also MSTP's home.
That is link aggregation, lesson 21.
That is MSTP, one tree per group of VLANs.
Right, later folded into 802.1D.

prompt: On a point-to-point cable, what lets RSTP put a port into forwarding in about a second instead of 30?
hint: It replaces the wait with a conversation.

choices.text: Shorter default timers
choices.why: RSTP keeps timers as a fallback; the speed comes from not waiting for them.

choices.text: A faster hello time of a tenth of a second
choices.why: Sending BPDUs faster would not tell a switch the far end is safe.

choices.text: A proposal and an agreement between the two
choices.why: Right. The far end makes sure it cannot loop, answers, and the port forwards.

choices.text: Skipping the root election on links between switches
choices.why: The election is the same as in 802.1D; RSTP changes how ports reach forwarding.

prompt: You want the core switch to be the root whatever MAC addresses the others have. What do you change on it?
hint: Lowest bridge ID wins, and one part of it is yours to set.

choices.text: Raise its priority to 61440
choices.why: Higher loses. The lowest bridge ID wins.

choices.text: Leave it at 32768 and replace it with a switch whose MAC is lower
choices.why: That works until a switch with a lower MAC arrives. A priority decides it on purpose.

choices.text: Lower the cost of its ports to 1
choices.why: Port cost shapes paths to the root; it does not choose which switch is the root.

choices.text: Lower its priority, to 4096 for instance
choices.why: Right. Priority is compared before the MAC, so the lower value wins outright.

prompt: A port that faces a computer, and goes straight to forwarding when a cable is plugged in, is configured as an ___ port.
hint: Cisco calls it PortFast.

prompt: BPDU guard was on for sw1's p10 when pc1 began sending BPDUs. What did bridge link show print for p10 six seconds later?
hint: The cable was still in.

choices.text: state blocking
choices.why: Blocking would still take part in the election. A guarded port leaves it.

choices.text: state disabled
choices.why: Right, with LOWER_UP still there: the link is fine, the port is shut.

choices.text: NO-CARRIER
choices.why: The signal was there. Disabling a port is not unplugging it.

choices.text: state forwarding, with pc1 as the new root
choices.why: That is what would happen without the guard, if pc1's ID were lower.

prompt: A desk port has BPDU filter on instead of BPDU guard. Somebody plugs a small switch into it and cables that switch to a second desk port, also filtered. What happens?
hint: What can a port learn from BPDUs it ignores?

choices.text: Both ports shut down when the switch's BPDUs arrive
choices.why: That is BPDU guard. A filter ignores the BPDUs rather than reacting to them.

choices.text: Spanning tree blocks one of the two desk ports
choices.why: To block, the switch would have to see its own BPDUs come back, and the filter discards them.

choices.text: A loop forms that spanning tree does not see, and a storm starts
choices.why: Right. Filtered ports hide the loop from the protocol meant to catch it.

choices.text: The small switch becomes root of the building
choices.why: Its BPDUs are filtered at the desk ports, so they do not reach the election.

prompt: Match each setting to what it does.
hint: Four tools, four different jobs.

pairs.right: Shuts the port when a BPDU arrives
Stops forwarding while a better root is announced
Caps the broadcast traffic a port accepts

prompt: A home switch with bridge priority 0 is plugged into an unprotected desk port. What is the likely result?
hint: 0 is the lowest priority there is.

choices.text: It wins the election and the tree reshapes around a desk
choices.why: Right. Traffic between distant switches then crosses it.

choices.text: The tree stays as it was, since a desk port is not part of it
choices.why: Without BPDU guard or root guard, a desk port takes part like any other.

choices.text: The desk port goes to state disabled
choices.why: That needs BPDU guard on the port, and this port is not set up with it.

choices.text: The core switch rejects it because 0 is not a valid priority
choices.why: 0 is valid, and it is the value that beats any default.

prompt: Which of these is a port state in RSTP but not in the original 802.1D?
hint: RSTP merged two states that forward nothing.

choices.text: discarding
choices.why: Right: blocking and listening merged into one.

choices.text: listening
choices.why: Listening is an 802.1D state, and RSTP folded it away.

choices.text: learning
choices.why: Learning exists in both.

choices.text: blocking
choices.why: Blocking is 802.1D's; RSTP calls it discarding.

prompt: Put the outcomes of the spanning-tree election in the order they are decided.
hint: Every later step is measured from the first.
items: A root port on each other switch
A designated port on each cable
trap: A root port before a root is impossible: "cheapest way to the root" needs a root to measure from.

prompt: After the priority change, sw3's bridge_id read 1000.02a59d312a8c. What is its priority in decimal?
hint: 1000 is hexadecimal.

prompt: A network runs classic STP with default priorities. Users lose calls for half a minute whenever an uplink fails. Which change addresses the cause?
hint: Where do the 30 seconds come from?

choices.text: Set forward delay to 2 seconds on each switch in the network
choices.why: That shortens the safety wait and risks a port forwarding before the tree settles, which is a loop.

choices.text: Turn on BPDU guard on the uplinks
choices.why: Uplinks face switches; guard there would shut them on the first BPDU.

choices.text: Run RSTP, so the alternate port takes over at once
choices.why: Right. The 30 seconds are listening and learning, which RSTP replaces.

choices.text: Lower the root's priority to 4096
choices.why: That chooses the root on purpose, which is good practice, but the wait after a failure is the same.
